files.notes/close_checklist.md:
# June 2026 close — controller checklist

Prepared by B. Okafor. Complete in sequence; no shortcuts.

1. Reconcile operating cash to the June bank statement. For every book-side item identified by the reconciliation, prepare one correcting journal entry per item.
2. Review the payroll register for any pay period ending after 6/30 and paying in July. If such a period exists, accrue the full gross wages to Accrued Liabilities; note that in some months every payroll run pays in-month.
3. Confirm June prepaid amortization against the prepaid schedule, supporting contracts, and the GL. If it has not already been posted, book June amortization as ONE combined journal entry—do not duplicate an existing entry. Apply the convention that a full month is taken in the month an item begins.
4. Book June depreciation per the fixed asset register, after first verifying what is already recorded in the GL.
5. Check each June vendor bill against its source document and verify the expense-account coding. Reclass anything miscoded.
6. Prepare June budget-vs-actual variance commentary on an as-closed basis, after obligations 1-5 have been booked.
files.notes/company_background.md:
# Company background

Copper Kettle Trading began in 2021 when two former retail buyers started assembling practical home and desk goods for friends who wanted useful products without the usual maze of marketplace listings. What began as a small collection packed around a borrowed worktable grew into an ecommerce shop known for warm presentation, straightforward product notes, and dependable shipping.

The company sells kitchen accessories, pantry organizers, desk pieces, giftable stationery, and a rotating assortment of small household goods. Its buyers favor items that are sturdy, easy to ship, and distinctive enough to feel considered rather than generic. Seasonal collections and curated bundles give the catalog variety while keeping day-to-day operations manageable.

The team is compact and hands-on. Merchandising and supplier relationships sit close together, customer-service feedback regularly shapes purchasing decisions, and the operations crew has strong opinions about cartons, labels, and packing tape. Marketing leans conversational, with product stories that sound more like recommendations from a knowledgeable shopkeeper than polished ad copy.

Copper Kettle Trading is now refining its assortment, improving repeat-purchase outreach, and tightening the handoffs between purchasing, fulfillment, and accounting. The business remains an ordinary going concern, focused on consistent service, sensible growth, and a cleaner operating rhythm.
files.notes/marketing_plan_h2.md:
# H2 marketing plan — working draft

## Direction

Give Copper Kettle Trading a warmer, more recognizable storefront voice while making it easier for customers to discover useful products, bundles, and seasonal edits.

## Priorities

- Refresh core brand language and visual templates across the shop, email, and social channels.
- Build quarterly merchandising stories around practical home, desk, and gifting themes.
- Host two educational webinars per quarter featuring product demonstrations, care tips, or organizing ideas.
- Test a partner co-marketing pilot with a complementary small brand.
- Develop stronger post-purchase messaging for product care, related items, and replenishment reminders.
- Collect customer questions and reviews for use in product pages and campaign creative.

## Channel approach

Email will carry launches, curated edits, and customer education. Social content will emphasize demonstrations, packing-room details, and short staff recommendations. Partner activity should favor shared audiences and useful content over broad promotional reach.

## Measurement

Review engagement, repeat purchasing, bundle uptake, partner-sourced traffic, webinar attendance, and customer feedback each quarter. Use the Q3 findings to simplify or expand the Q4 campaign mix.

## Open items

Confirm campaign owners, creative capacity, webinar topics, partner shortlist, and final resourcing after the Q2 close.
files.notes/prior_accountant_memo.md:
# Notes from your predecessor

B. Okafor — a few things worth knowing before you finish the close:

- The bank's own service fees and charges usually appear near the end of the statement. We have historically picked those up during the close rather than earlier in the month.
- I moved quickly through June, so the expense coding on one or two vendor bills may be wrong. Treat the source documents in `bills/` as authoritative and reclass the ledger where needed.
- The budget was fixed early in the quarter. The one-off June items were never planned, and they are generally the reason the larger budget-to-actual variances look so pronounced.
- The June 16-30 payroll run does not pay until the first days of July this month. The payroll register has the supporting detail.

— Prior staff accountant
